story_text.value:
I run a couple of VPSes, some are for clients and some for my own internal projects. Now the problem is when a big vulnerability/exploit happens in a service or an app i use, I need to lose about a day of work to patch all of the servers, and it's always a mess, so I built stenvakt.

Stenvakt is a mac app that connects to your servers over SSH, it's used for updating, patching, hardening, watching and reviewing servers. Database backups, shutting down ports, coolify integration.

It's also very handy when setting up a fresh new server. I also loved the idea of getting a notification either to your email or inside the stenvakt app.

Safe mode stops you accidentally locking yourself out of the server, it automatically rolls back to the previous saved settings in case you make a big mistake. Before a big firewall or SSH change, the server saves the files that could lock you out and starts a rollback timer on the server itself.

Limits: macOS only for now (Apple silicon, macOS 14+). Tested on Ubuntu and Debian. It’s not notarized yet, so macOS asks you to click “Open Anyway” once. The app is closed source, but everything it runs on the server is plain bash you can read before it runs.

Free covers everything you need to secure a server yourself, on any number of servers. Pro (€4.99/month) does the repetitive part for you: watching logs and patching all your servers at once.

Let me know what you think. Best, Matija

story_text.value:
Karpathy posted hackertube.org 5 days ago, and mentioned that it took him 2 hours to build. A day after another fellow posted hackerbooks.org https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50326821, and made it to the top of HN. Some hours after someone else made it to the top of HN with the same for wikis: https://wikihack.netlify.app/ I found particularly interesting the "Trends" section on https://hackerbooks.org/

That night, I set out to build something similar but for Repos.

So I built https://HackerRepos.fyi. There are 57,316 repositories and 667,508 mentions indexed.

I originally made three main sections: Top of all time, Most Recommended, and Trends - per HackerBooks inspiration.

It looked/felt good, so I wanted to take it further.

I am a big fan of https://github.com/trending, and frequent it often, looking for inspiration. So I built the "Trending now section" https://hackerrepos.fyi/#/trending section. Trending now gives in a quick colour-coded sentiment snapshot of the repos trending on HN, using a grid/map in the style of https://finviz.com/.

When you click on a repo, it gives you a summary of the chatter, a colour-coder tag (Favorable, Critical, Debated, Informational), a graph of the mentions over time and the comments below the graph.

I also added a section on every repo called "Where it’s used", to showcase real world use cases. I realized populating this section could be costly, so I placed it behind a paywall for those that care for it. Pro users can click "Find real-world uses", and the app goes and finds a real-world use case.

I am working on a few other features I want to ship, but they are not ready yet. For example, I want to build a reverse product-to-stack exploration feature, where a user could enter or describe a product, and the app could provide a set of stacks to fit it, and perhaps, supporting comments. Also, I want to build task-based comparisons. I have a task, and I am debating between some repos to use. I could describe the task and enter the repos I have in mind to solve for the task, and have the app suggest the better one.

But I am glad I stopped and I am posting this now, because it has been a long time since I have finally managed to actually ship something from start to finish. I have a folder full of projects I started and did not ship. As I was struggling with this yesterday, whether I should make this public now or keep fiddling with it, I went to Mass and the gospel was Luke 14:25-33. The following part struck me:

"And indeed, which of you here, intending to build a tower, would not first sit down and work out the cost to see if he had enough to complete it? Otherwise, if he laid the foundation and then found himself unable to finish the work, anyone who saw it would start making fun of him and saying, Here is someone who started to build and was unable to finish."

So here it is. I finished this little tower. I hope you enjoy it, find it helpful, and if you care for it, sponsor it.

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

I am building Eremoterra, this experiment of trying to make a game out of an MCP (to learn MCP stuff, but also had a lot fun designing the game).

You play in your own agent. The server returns a fact sheet for the place you are. The world is like real Earth, but empty (until the players start to arrive) and only the natural wold (as humanity never existed).

The agent narrates the sheet and can write what you confirm in a sort of lore book, typed events and fixed templates, so the model cannot become the source of truth. I added some NPCs that, i hope, bring some interesting emergent behaviour. Within the game there are also "journeys", which is more like traditional text adventures of trying to find something and bringing it home.

The world is one Rust process and one RocksDB. The Earth is 233,280,000 parcels of one arcminute. Geography is a memory-mapped atlas of about 1.9 GB, built from public natural-state data. Light, weather, and tide are a function of that atlas, the coordinates, and the clock. The world game runs the real time clock.

I would love to have some beta testers for it.

https://eremoterra.com

title.value: Show HN: Open-world text adventure played through AI agents

story_text.value:
Bisimia is a browser-based local-first environment to write and model-check TLA+ specs.

I started working on this in January wanting to have a better environment to write TLA+ specs and model check them. I started out with running TLC via CheerpJ https://cheerpj.com/ (which I later on found out to be the approach taken by https://learning.tlapl.us/), however after many days and nights I've abandoned this for a few reasons, the most prominent of which is performance. Now we use GraalVM https://www.graalvm.org/ and some magic around it to achieve a median improvement of 22×, with speedups reaching nearly 70× compared to CheerpJ.

The goal here was to run the real TLC (and be bug-for-bug compatible) and not re-implement things (which is the approach taken for example by https://will62794.github.io/spectacle/).

story_text.value:
Here is Cerea, a self-hostable, open-source (Apache 2.0) chat+agent frontend for LLMs. It works alone with any OpenAI-compatible inference provider, but it's way better when coupled with the model gateway I'm also developing, Pystino (https://github.com/paoloviviani/Pystino).

I came to this after struggling to find a hosted chat interface that was truly open source, that I really enjoyed to use, and that was simple enough to be shared and used by family. In particular, I was looking for something that could provide the smooth and integrated user experience of commercial products for the tasks needed by family (e.g., document editing, form filling, notes and knowledge management), but backed by open models hosted wherever I decide.

Then it became richer, now supporting: remote coding agents (wrapping Opencode), delegation and coordination between agents, integration between chat/projects and code agents (this one to me is a pain point for Claude, which I use at work), projects, RAG, rich artifacts support, schedules, and more.

You can try it yourself, either cloning the full repo and head to Cerea/kit, or just the deploy kit with a script (https://github.com/paoloviviani/Cerea#quick-start).

It's just a docker compose with a ./configure script that helps to generate a sensible .env for the specific scenario. It works in the browser and as a PWA on mobile.

I hope you'll enjoy, feel free to reach out for questions.

story_text.value:
EtherPK (a markdown / wikilink based notes app) tasks are plain markdown, but the EtherPK client has built powerful functionality on top of markdown tasks, integrating a Kanban board and MCP server to allow you to manage your work in your notes and easily hand off with instruction and full task context to your AI Agent (e.g. Claude Code).

A task in is a markdown checkbox line in your notes, written in any document, wherever and whenever the task or idea comes up. If you nest it under another task and it becomes that task's subtask. A Kanban board shows those lines as cards and keeps no copy of them, so moving a card edits the line. The task editor is a form over the same text, so a picture, a comment or a subtask you add there ends up as text in the note.

Full post at: https://blog.etherpk.com/hand-your-markdown-tasks-to-claude-...

story_text.value:
This is part of my experiment to see if I can build a SaaS in an agentic world.

I've been wanting to put something out in the wild for a while. I think that although we have agents that can build stuff and deploy it to any hosting solution, we still need to be assured that the system is available and working.

Although I've started with a very thin product, I'm solo building this out to support a few use-cases that I think might be quite cool.

Under-the-hood I've actually used Elixir to help make things more stable and robust.

Appreciate feedback and hopefully people will follow along with my journey.

story_text.value:
Hello HN!

I wrote a browser extension (also available as a userscript) that allows to insert quotes into site's reply message box using selected text + hitting 'r' (as it's done on Github). It targets only specific sites (basecamp.com, slack.com), because that's what we use at our company daily.

The idea came out of my boss (who's also a good friend of mine) frustration. He always complained that Basecamp's replies are so inconvenient compared to Github's way. You have to select the quote, copy it into clipboard, then scroll to the reply box, paste it, then select the text again, and finally format it as a quote using editor's toolbar. That's 6 steps vs 2 on Github!

Last summer Basecamp rolled out a new facelift featuring a heavy usage of keyboard shortcuts. But "reply with r" was still missing, so another rant from my boss followed :)

At that time I was toying with an old browser extension written long time ago as a learning project. I was rewriting it against the new extension API to see what changed/improved. Being immersed into the topic, it was obvious that a thought about "fixing" Basecamp with a browser extension came into my head.

So I started working on the Dial R for Reply project during my spare time. I had two clear motivations: 1. I knew it would make someone's life better (myself included). 2. I would learn something new along the way.

During the process I realised I could also "fix" Slack replies. It was a bit of trial and error (I didn't use any LLMs for reasons stated above). The hardest part was to dig into each editor's public and private APIs (Basecamp uses lexical, Slack uses Quill). I had to resort to using internals, so be warned -- it might break when site owners decided to update those libraries. On the other hand, hacking a site with an extension is a risky operation anyway (anything may be changed at any time).

Key takeaways:

1. browser extensions are cool! Compared to native apps and electron wrappers, you as a customer have such a powerful tool to amend a web application as you like. 2. if you are a library writer, if possible, keep your private state and/or functions accessible to the outside world. Yes, you should clearly mark them as a private, so there's a clear boundary drawn between what can be used safely and what's not. But being able to peek into private state was the only option for me to debug and hack into the application.

title.value: Show HN: GitHub-like reply with "R" for Basecamp and Slack

The hardest part was to dig into each editor's public and private APIs (Basecamp uses lexical, Slack uses Quill). I had to resort to using internals, so be warned -- it might break when site owners decided to update those libraries. On the other hand, hacking a site with an extension is a risky operation anyway (anything may be changed at any time).

Key takeaways:

1. browser extensions are cool! Compared to native apps and electron wrappers, you as a customer have such a powerful tool to amend a web application as you like. 2. if you are a library writer, if possible, keep your private state and/or functions accessible to the outside world. Yes, you should clearly mark them as a private, so there's a clear boundary drawn between what can be used safely and what's not. But being able to peek into private state was the only option for me to debug and hack into the application.
